data.text/markdown:
Week 3 — Build your aggregator

An aggregator is one table, at one grain, that joins several public sources and records where every column came from. Yours is at hospital grain: one row per hospital. You will keep this notebook all term — every later week (verify, defend, app, agent, refresh) starts from the layer it builds. The build, in order:
  1. Start with every hospital in CMS Hospital General Information.
  2. Join one measure from CMS Unplanned Hospital Visits (you pick it).
  3. (optional) Join HRRP, the readmissions penalty program, for the same condition.
  4. (optional) Join county measures (CDC PLACES and/or ACS) through the course crosswalk.
After every step the join ledger counts the rows. If a number changes and you can't say why, stop — that is the lesson for tonight.

data.text/html:
Your choices

Clear both county lists to build a hospital-only layer.

data.text/markdown:
The build (read this code — it is the lesson)

This is the only code you are asked to read this week. The explanation is under it.

data.text/html:
• ledger = [] — an empty list. Every step below adds one line to it: that list is the join ledger.
  • def count(step, df, kind, matched=None) — a small helper that writes down the step's name, how many rows the table has now, how many different hospitals, and how many rows found a match. It hands the table back unchanged.
  • layer = hospitals[[...]] — start from every hospital, keeping five columns. This is the grain: one row per Facility ID.
  • layer.merge(uv_rows, on="Facility ID", how="left", ...) — a left join: keep every hospital on the left; attach the measure where the Facility ID matches; leave it blank where it doesn't. Nothing is thrown away, and nothing is filled in with zero.
  • validate="one_to_one" — a guard. If either side had a Facility ID twice, the join would multiply rows; this line makes pandas stop with an error instead of silently duplicating hospitals.
  • if only_scored.value: layer = layer[...notna()] — the only step that removes rows, and only if you ticked the box. The ledger shows how many.
  • The HRRP join works the same way, on the same key.
  • The crosswalk join adds a county_fips column to each hospital. Then PLACES and ACS join on county_fips with validate="many_to_one": many hospitals can share one county, but each county must appear only once on the right.
  • matched=...notna().sum() — counts rows where the new source actually supplied something. Rows staying the same while rows matched drops is how a left join tells you what it couldn't find.

Join ledger

A left join should never change rows. If it does, the right-hand table had a duplicate key. A filter should change rows, and the ledger says by how much.

What didn't match, and why

629 hospitals have no READM_30_HF row at all (kept in the layer, left blank). By hospital type:
1,537 of 4,790 READM_30_HF rows have a score that is not a number. They stay missing in uv_score_num; the original text stays in uv_score.
20 HRRP rows for READM-30-HF-HRRP have a Facility ID that is not in Hospital General Information. A left join from hospitals drops them. Who are they?
Only 3,035 of 5,419 hospitals have an HRRP row. HRRP does not cover every kind of hospital. Which types are in it? Check the HRRP source page for the rule before you write it down.
The crosswalk could not place these hospitals in a CDC county. Territories are not in the CDC county files; 'check by hand' rows are CMS spellings that didn't match.
325 hospitals have a county FIPS that PLACES 2025 doesn't have. Connecticut is one: the crosswalk uses the old counties (Fairfield County = 09001); PLACES reports CT as planning regions (Capitol, Greater Bridgeport, Lower Connecticut River Valley, Naugatuck Valley, Northeastern Connecticut, Northwest Hills, South Central Connecticut, Southeastern Connecticut, Western Connecticut). Look at the other states too, then check the PLACES source page before you explain them.

Checks your layer reruns on every refresh

These run every time the notebook runs — when you change a choice above, and in week 12 when a source is refreshed. They are the layer's backpressure: if a source changes under you, a check fails instead of a wrong number reaching your app. You set the match-rate bar; the AI can't decide what's good enough for your question.

Your layer

5,419 rows × 26 columns. Blank cells are missing values, not zeros. Column prefixes say where each column came from: uv_ unplanned visits, hrrp_ HRRP, places_ CDC PLACES, acs_ ACS, county_/match_note the course crosswalk.
